mythic_age.village.say.festival.polis_fe: It's the Polis Festival — follow the basket up to the altar.
This evening we dance in the square, hand in hand in a long chain.
The festival is tomorrow. Tonight torch-runners carry the fire from the village gate to the altar.
mythic_age.village.say.festival.rural_di: The Dionysia! Wine jars in front, the piper close behind.
There's a play this afternoon — the actors all wear masks.
The Rural Dionysia is tomorrow — time to open the new wine.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.bronzesmith: Bronze is copper with about a tenth part tin — too little and it's soft, too much and it's brittle.
Two of us take turns on the bellows to keep the fire hot enough.
For a casting you make it in wax, coat it in clay and fire it, then pour the bronze where the wax ran out.
Once the blade is cast it's hammered cold — that's what hardens bronze.
Our patron Hephaestus worked his forge on a lame leg too.
Tin comes from very far away — the traders say across several seas.
No tin, no fire in the furnace.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.farmer.chat: We knock the olives down with long poles onto cloths spread underneath.
Olive trees grow slowly — you plant them for your grandchildren.
We reap the wheat with sickles, then winnow it on the threshing floor so the wind carries off the chaff.
When the grapes ripen the whole household picks, then we tread them in the vat.
The first pressing gives the best oil — for lamps, for cooking, for the skin.
The olives need pruning, and the cuttings go to feed the kiln.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.farmer.shor: Food is running low — for now it's harvesting and baking first.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.hoplite.cha: A helmet and breastplate guard yourself; the shield guards the whole line.
Forearm through the band, hand on the grip at the rim — then even a heavy shield stays up.
Off duty I work the fields too — the spear is a citizen's, and so is the plough.
When someone prays at the altar, I stand between them and the danger.
Spear low on the approach; once you close, raise it over the shoulder and thrust.
Someone watches the village gate through the night — sleep easy.
We go light and run fast — that's the whole of our art.
Throw, step back three paces, throw again. The heavy men can't catch us.
The old men say it was folk like us who pinned the Spartans down at Sphacteria.
When enemies come I fan the sacred brazier first — then the whole village knows.
After a fight we gather the javelins; the good ones go back to the granary.
Fire signals leap from peak to peak — they say that's how the fall of Troy was told.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.laborer.cha: Hauled stone all day; tomorrow it's off to the woods.
Whatever the village is short of, the steward sends us to do.
At harvest there are never enough hands — everyone goes to the fields.
Fell one, plant one — that way the woods never run out.
When the jars in the granary are full, winter holds no fear.
Evenings I sit in the square and hear the news from outside.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.laborer.sho: Nothing urgent on hand; waiting for the steward's word.
Cut a row of wedge holes, drive in wooden wedges and wet them — the wood swells and the stone splits along the line.
A column isn't one piece — it's a stack of drums.
There's no mortar between the blocks — iron clamps hold them, and lead is poured into the joints.
The fluting is carved only after the column is standing in place.
Blocks are roughed out with a protective skin left on, and finished only at the site.
You can tell from the sound of the chisel whether the stone has a flaw.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.mason.short: The quarry is worked out — without marble there's nothing to do but wait.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.merchant.ch: The market wardens check the scales and weights — short measure gets you fined.
Foreign coins have to go through the money changer before you can spend them here.
Wine travels by ship in amphoras, the mouths sealed with clay.
The sea route is far quicker than the donkey road — if the weather holds.
It's cool under the stoa — traders and idlers alike gather here.
Hermes looks after traders — and thieves too, so I lock up at night.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.merchant.sh: The goods haven't arrived yet — come back in a few days.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.potter.chat: Clay has to be soaked and left to settle until the grit is gone before it goes on the wheel.
My apprentice turns the wheel; I only shape the pot.
Firing goes in three stages: air in to redden it, air shut off to blacken it, then air in again.
The terracotta tiles overlap on the rafters, and the rain runs off down the channels.
A sound pot rings when you tap it; a cracked one sounds dull.
The workshop sits by the clay pit to save carrying.
mythic_age.village.say.greek.potter.shor: The clay pit is dug out; we'll have to wait a few days.
